caption_en: 4. Atrium (b), trapezoidal E, face E: relief with the wild boar attacked by a dog that jumped on its back. The group closely resembles, due to the characteristics of the dog, the bronze group of the Casa del Citarista (I 4, 5.25), a fountain ornament in which a wild boar is attacked by two dogs (now in the Museo Naz. in Naples, inv. 4899, 4900, 4901). 79 N51216

6. Atrium (b), trapezophore E, face O with the representation of a dog advancing at a pace, with the front left exaggeratedly raised, under an oak tree in which the shape of the leaves is close to reality, although they are not at all proportionate to the width of the foliage, and the whole tree is not proportionate to the dog.

7. Atrium (b), trapezoid O, face O: the subject is the same as the support E but was clearly executed by a different hand: the details of the dog and especially of the oak reveal greater rigidity and less fidelity to reality. The plant is certainly an oak due to the presence of acorns, but the leaves are closer to those of plane trees, and the trunk looks rather like a branch.
8. Atrium (b), trapezoid O, face O: detail of the relief with dog and oak.

9. Atrium (b), wall O: in the S section, under the staircase to the upper floor, there is a lararium niche that inside the vault with a white background presented, painted in blue and red, birds resting on leafy branches of which traces of flowers now remain.

10. Oecus (c): evident in the N wall is the door that once opened onto the street and was walled up when the workshop room was transformed into a retreat room with a rather simple IV style decoration. On the black plinth, the middle area with a white background was divided into panels with taut carpets (?), in each of which there was a small square, on the sides of a shrine. The stucco frame was in various colors.

11. Oecus (c): through the door on the S wall you can see the columns of the tetrastyle atrium, covered with smooth stucco in the lower part and grooved in the upper two-thirds, pertaining to the original layout of the house. The hoof is black.
12. Oecus(c), wall O: white middle area with panels with a triangle carpet edge.
13. Triclinium (d): in the cocciopesto floor with sparse scattered white tesserae, near the threshold there was a mat with the exhortation CEDO CENEMUS, which has now completely disappeared.

14. Triclinium (d), N wall: in the III style decoration, in the centre of the short sides, aedicules framed by white columns with large paintings with a large red border could be recognised. While that of the S wall was already lost at the time of the excavation, that of the opposite N wall with a sacral landscape was described by Mau (BdI, 1873) and reproduced in pencil by G. Discanno in 1872 (see fig. below). The side panels were black, as was the frieze above, whose figurative subjects had already vanished. 79 N51201

15. Triclinium (d), N wall: the painting (1.70 x 1.10 m), now completely disappeared, documented by G. Discanno and by a watercolour by DAIR of 1885, represented a sacellum whose roof is supported by a herm of Dionysus with thyrsus and kantharos. Inside there is the statue of a seated female deity, identified as Artemis for the radiated crown she wears on her head and for the presence of a bow, quiver, spear and another radiated crown suspended from a betylus placed at the back of the building. On the left there is a man in a tunic and chlamys, with boots and hat who, leaning on a stick with his left arm, extends his right towards the temple. Apart from the trees that are strictly part of the scene, the background was white, as is typical of the paintings of the second phase of the III style (cf. Draftsmen, p. 858, fig. 27).
16. Triclinium (d), S wall with red plinth; in the black middle z0na the predella can be identified with a square placed at the corner and another, partly vanished, placed straight. 79 N51190
17. Cubicle (f), N wall: on the black plinth, the white middle area had a bipartite structure with panels bordered by groups of thin lines of different colours.

19. Kitchen (g): the cylindrical altar of red stucco, rendered as a Doric semi-column, around which the yellow-painted agathodemon serpent was wrapped three times, was placed under the Lares with situla and rhytòn; on the lower left was painted a two-handled pot on a tripod under which a flame was lit, on the right a pig's head, a spit with pieces of meat and sausages skewered; higher up there was a scriptoria tablet from which the text once written there had been erased. The lararium as a whole was framed by a red line and surmounted by three tapeworms, probably arranged, as in many other cases, in a festoon.

18. Kitchen (g): the masonry counter with the wood storage compartment below is leaning against the N wall; the flooring was made of large rectangular bricks. On the wall E protrudes the stucco altar in relief around which a snake wraps itself.

21. Tablinum (h): the ancient structure in opus quadrata of tuff, in which a narrow splayed window opened, is preserved in the S wall; of ancient restoration is the upper part in uncertain work with a recourse of bricks.   79 N51206
20. Kitchen (g), wall E: the altar shelf consists of two tiles and an offering of fruit rested on it.  79 N51221

22. Tablinum (h), wall O: in the S section there remains a short section of the black plinth articulated in panels with plants, and of the white middle area with a panel bordered by thin red and black lines.
23. Room (i), wall O: discoloured plinth.

24. Courtyard (1): in the N wall, in opus reticulata, in the O section there is a circular window in the thickness of which the fragments of the closing glass plate, concave towards the inside of the room (m), are preserved.

25. Cubicle (m): on the N wall there are traces of the III style decoration with a white background with purple vertical bands for a stretch of the middle area in correspondence, probably, with a wardrobe that was leaning against it. The upper area was instead tapped to make a new layer of plaster adhere; of the fourth style remake the purple plinth and part of the black middle area remain.

26. Cubicle (m), wall E: the original fresco of the III style had a black plinth, the middle white area divided by purple vertical bands into panels, in the center of which were small squares (27 x 47 cm) framed in green. The entire surface was tapped for the application of the most recent plaster painted in the fourth style with a red plinth with plants and a red middle area.

27. Cubicle (m), wall E: the S section largely preserved the decoration of the IV style with the red plinth divided into panels with plants, separated by very narrow compartments and the middle area, also with red panels separated by a twisted candelabrum, with a border of a triangle carpet and squares with birds and fruit.

28. Cubicle (m), S wall with the large quadrangular window and the circular one above, which exclude the use of the room as a bedroom, although on the floor, near this same wall, the traces of a Kline were preserved.
29. Cubicle (m), wall O with traces of wardrobe in the N section: the plinth and the middle area are red.

Above a simple black plinth, still in the tradition of the III 'severe' style, the wall has an overabundance of miniaturist decorative elements, which reveal its belonging to the final phase of this style. The centre of the wall completely attracts the viewer's attention because of the large aedicule and the painting it contains (see fig. below). 2. The painting, representing the intoxication of Hercules at Omphale (H, 1137, now in the Museum of Naples, inv. 9000), emphasizes the power of wine and Dionysus, and could suggest that the environment of origin was used as a triclinium.

3. From the same room comes the painting depicting the liberation of Andromeda by Perseus. Helbig, who describes the painting on the basis of the text in PAH (H, 1189), considers it destroyed: it is instead identifiable with the one in the Museum of Naples (inv. 8997; H, 1187; cf. Disegnatori, p. 402, fig. 225), and it is therefore referred to in the comparison by Bianchi Bandinelli cited in fig. previous.

4. Illucido by G. Abbate (cfr. Disegnatori, pp. 400-401, figs. 222-224) reproduces the painting with the Rape of Europa (H, 123), now lost. 1. The façade of the house on Vicolo dei Soprastanti: the sidewalk is covered with cocciopesto and the large and short vestibule has a travertine threshold; the masonry, in place on a frame with jambs in large limestone blocks, retains fragments of plaster.
2. The façade of the house on Vicolo dei Soprastanti, seen from the N

3. Vestibule (1), black and white mosaic floor: the room is notable for its unusual proportions; it is in fact wider than it is long. A frame consisting of a simple and low black band frames the complicated plant motif, obtained with very slender elements, symmetrically arranged on the two sides of a horizontal element. The floor, with its light vegetal ornamentation typical of the repertoire of the III style, can be dated to the early imperial age and is older than the black-background floor of the atrium.

4. Vestibule (1), N wall with remains of a fresco of the second style almost completely illegible (on the left, at the corner, a pilaster can be glimpsed), but most likely brought to light in this state: Fiorelli in fact (cited in the bibl.) describes on this wall and on the one in front of it 'two ancient paintings that have now completely vanished'.
5. Vestibule (1), S wall with remains of a fresco of the second style; the passage to the atrium is underlined by a slightly raised pilaster.

6. Atrium (2), view from the W (from the tablinum towards the vestibule) with the high and narrow openings of the surrounding rooms — typical of the first style installations — bordered by jambs in limestone blocks. At the center of the vast room is the impluvium, without cladding slabs (Eschebach, cited in the bibliography, speaks of an impluvium in limestone slabs).

7. Atrium (2), view of the N side: in the center the wing (6), flanked by the doors of the rooms (7) and (5); on the left are visible the column that emphasizes the entrance to the tablinum (9) and the high door (walled) that connected the atrium with the room (8). The masonry is in situ with a frame of limestone blocks, the wall common with the house at no. 15 is instead in opus incerta with recourse to bricks. '79 N60979

8. Atrium (2), view of the S side, with the wing (14) flanked by the doors of the rooms (15), (13) and (11). The masonry is in place with a frame of large blocks of limestone and bears only scant remains of cladding.

9. Atrium (2), SW section of the impluvium: detail of the floor with a carpet of small black tesserae arranged in a straight warp, punctuated with scattered white tesserae, mixed with flakes and slabs of polychrome marble. According to Pernice (cited in the bibl.) the impluvium was underlined by a polychrome braid. The floor can be assigned to the late Republican age.

10. Atrium (2), detail of the floor at the threshold of the room (8), subsequently walled up: the opening does not seem to be respected by the flooring, which does not have the edge and the high marginal flounce visible on the right on this side. 79 N60855

11. Atrium (2), section N-W with the travertine threshold of the room (7): detail of the floor (carpet of black tesserae arranged in an oblique warp with white tesserae and densely scattered coloured marble slabs; the edge has a white band between two black bands and a high marginal flounce of black tesserae arranged in an oblique warp). II style.

12. Atrium (2), N-E corner with the travertine threshold of the room (5): detail of the mosaic floor assignable to the II style (of which the preparation emerges), covered by the brick podium of the lararium.

13. Atrium (2), N wall, section E: the podium of the lararium rests on the mosaic floor datable to the II style and covers a remnant of wall decoration that Mau (Mau W, p. 281) assigns to the same phase.  79 N60981

14. Wing (6). The floor of this room can also be assigned to the second style, with its extremely sober ornamentation: a beaten white flakes in which scant remains of the typical late Republican ornamentation with crosses (much more frequent in cocciopesto carpets) are preserved, here made 'in negative', black with a white center. The beaten ends in correspondence with the contemporary mosaic floor of the atrium, with a low flounce of black tesserae arranged in a straight warp.  79 N60849

15. Room (8), wall E, section S with walled door: the wall preserves the rest of a first style plan made in stucco relief at the top. On the infill of the door are the remains of a fresco that Mau (Mau W, p. 96) assigns to the second style.

16. Tablinum (9), view from the E, towards the peristyle (18): the room still retains the layout of the Republican age, with the high columns (consisting of three-quarters of a column) in deeply fluted limestone and covered with white stucco, like the Corinthian capital, which came out (cf. Lauter-Bufe 1987, cited in bibl.) from the same workshop that executed those intended for the last public buildings of the Samnite city. The tall, narrow doors that connected rooms (8) and (10) with the atrium (2) were plugged. According to Mau (Mau W, p. 281) the plinth of the room had been restored in the third style.

17. Wing (14): the floor is coeval with that of the wing in front (6) (see fig. 14), a white beaten with regular dotted crosses of black tesserae (barely recognizable in the section in front of the wall), bordered by a row of tesserae of the same color, placed together at the vertices in a rather loose manner.

18. Wing (14), wall E: in the masonry we can recognize the infill of the two (?) doors that connected the rooms (14) and (15), covered with a fresco datable, according to Mau's testimony (Mau W, p. 96), to the II style.

19. Wing (14): a door has also been walled up in the S wall of the room, which communicated with the entrance hall at no. 12. This transformation precedes the wall decoration of the second style, now completely illegible, of which a fragment (in the same state) is also preserved on the O wall.

20. Cubicle (16), NE corner with remains of a yellow plane attributable to the oldest decorative phase attested in the house (I style); the room was covered by a fake cross vault, the remains of which can be seen here, above the relief plan.
21. Cubicle (16), S wall: remains of first-style wall coverings, with white upper area, yellow top and the white lunette of the false cross vault.
22. Peristyle (18): view from the N with a swimming pool in the centre of the open area and Ionic columns in fluted tuff covered with white stucco, dating back to the Republican period.
23. Peristyle (18): remains of the white travertine floor, enlivened by scattered flakes of coloured limestone, coeval with the architectural layout of the room. 79 N51024
24. Room (30), cocciopesto floor in which black and white tiles are scattered, dating back to the Republican age (I century BC ?).

25. Room (30): the S-E corner preserves the remains of a wall covering with a black plinth, simply enlivened by splashes of purple and yellow and bordered at the top by a high purple band, above which the middle area is white. The lack of typological elements does not allow a certain dating of the decoration, which can probably be assigned to the first century AD.

26. Triclinium (31), floor: in the cocciopesto carpet are densely scattered, in apparent disorder, the typical rectangular tesserae of the second style, black and white and in green limestone, which stop regularly a few centimetres from the edge, consisting of a row of alternating black and white tesserae, bedded at the vertices and slightly spaced, and the smooth marginal flounce.

27. Triclinium (31), wall N, section O: the wall decoration can be framed in a scheme of the III style; nevertheless, it cannot be said with certainty that it was redone at a later stage than that of the floor arrangement, as we cannot exclude that it is the intentional choice of a more 'modernizing' decoration than that attested, for example, in the adjacent cubicle (32) (see figs. 37-43).

28. Triclinium (31), N wall, W section, antechamber: detail of the small picture with a sacral landscape in the centre of the black middle area. Figurines of bidders can be glimpsed quickly sketched in front of a low open fence (schola). III style.

29. Triclinium (31), N wall, central section (antechamber): remains of the black middle area marked by a column and surmounted by a frieze containing a series of small floral elements spaced out, a typical ornament of walls that can be assigned as this one straddling the schemes of the II style and those of III.

31. Triclinium (31), wall E (room): remains of a fresco with a black background with a central aedicule supported by miniaturist ornate columns (the one on the right is visible). Above the upper area, also black, you can see the clamps for fixing a stucco frame. The fresco of the III style rests on a cavity whose upper layer is composed of large fragments of amphorae, behind which the remains of an older wall covering (in the II style schematiCOP) can be glimpsed.

30. Triclinium (31), N wall, section E with the decoration of the room: the plinth was simply adorned with splashes of color (green, purple and yellow); in the black middle area you can see the pillar that marks the partition between the antechamber and the hall and, barely legible, two palm trunks. The frieze and the upper area, which has not been completely cleaned, are also black.

32. Triclinium (31), wall E, section S: below the upper black area, adorned with a tripod, in the frieze also black you can see an ornament from the initial phase of the III style, small floral elements — almost gems -, spaced out from each other and framed by a crenellated motif.

33. Triclinium (31), S wall, section E (room): remains of a fresco of the III style. The plinth is adorned with splashes of colour; black middle area with palm trunks supporting the tympanum of the central aedicule (barely legible in the upper area), a dividing pillar between the antechamber and the hall. Above the black frieze, in the upper black area, a figure can be seen (see fig. below).
34. Triclinium (31), S wall, section E: upper black area with an Egyptian figure (recognizable by the short crossed robe) holding a situla. III style.
35. Triclinium (31): sporadic fragment of a stucco frame with a high smooth band surmounted by mouldings (pertinent to the environment?).

36. Cubicle (32), antechamber: the cocciopesto floor with ornamentation outlined in white tesserae and sparse black tesserae is certainly coeval with that of the adjacent triclinium (31) and, like the latter, bears a typical ornamentation of the II style, the network of staircase meanders alternating with squares with a central cross of black and white tesserae. The border is also made up of black and white tiles.

37. Cubicle (32), N wall, section O (antechamber): the room has a decorative scheme of the second style, based on the imitation of a marble incrustation. Despite this, it cannot be said with certainty that it is an older wall decoration than that of the adjacent triclinium (31): the difference in schemes could respond to a choice of the client; the state of conservation of the painting makes it impossible to judge whether it is a lingering decoration (of the type attested, for example, in the House of Trebius Valens, III 2, l:cf. vol. III, pp. 356-357, figs. 2224).

38. Cubicle (32), N wall, section O (antechamber): wall with 'closed' pattern of the second style; The wall is imagined to be covered with coloured marble slabs variously arranged, so that it is always recognisable both the division into three horizontal areas (plinth, middle and upper area) and the distinction between antechamber and alcove, underlined here by the dividing pillar with mirrors visible on the right of the photo. 79 N50993
39. Cubicle (32), N wall, section E: alcove with wall covering of the second style.

40. Cubicle (32), wall E: the small alcove is covered by a false vault and preserves scarce remains of the fresco of the second style. The large hole in the wall signals the passage in this area of prospectors, who entered here in an unspecified period (in ancient times or in the Bourbon era?). 79 N50995
42. Cubicle (32), S wall, section E (alcove): remains of a fresco of the second style.
41. Cubicle (32), wall E, section N: detail of the lunette with a simple moulded stucco frame, typical of the II style.
43. Cubicle (32), S wall, section O: remains of the II style decoration of the antechamber, not completely freed from volcanic material.

44. Room (35): the cocciopesto bottom of the floor is almost completely covered with black and white tiles and scales, which in some places seem to hint at a cross pattern. Like the other floors of the house, this one must also be assignable to the II style and datable to the first century BC.
46. Room (35), S wall with the door and window communicating with the room (36): black plinth adorned with splashes of color; black middle area, yellow frieze; white upper area.

45. Room (35), wall E with 'candelabra' style III decoration [contemporary with that of the surrounding rooms (31) and (32) ?]. In this room, as in the triclinium (see Fig. 30), the black plinth is adorned with splashes of white and red. The middle area, also black, is punctuated by garlands hanging from columns, a motif derived from the schemes of the second style, in which, however, all the elements are characterized by a great plasticity that must make the architectural illusion credible, here completely abandoned in favor of a conception of the wall as a flat and closed surface to be covered with minute and elegant decorations. The frieze
48. Room (35), wall O, section S: in the continuous band plinth the only scansion is made up of the slender candelabra typical of this phase.
47. Room (35), wall W with remains of a fresco (III 'candelabra' style).

49. The fragments collapsed to the ground and protected from the sun reveal individual details of the decoration of the upper white area of the room (35), which was punctuated by architecture: here are the remains of a triangular tympanum.

50. Room (35): collapsed fragments of the upper white area, belonging to an aedicule like the one in fig. of which they reproduce the same ornaments. The female figure in acroterial function is frequent on walls datable like this one between the II and III style.
51. Room (35): detail of the architectural elements of the upper white area (collapsed fragments).

52. Room (35): these fragments of the decoration of the upper area also have some characteristic elements that allow us to date the decoration to the very first years of the imperial age, in a period very close to that in which the decorations of the Roman villa of the Farnesina were carried out (cf. Bragantini - De Vos 1982).
53. Fragments of decoration (III style with candelabra) pertaining to the upper area of the room (35).
55. Among the fragments of fresco that collapsed from the upper area of the room (35) there is another canopy element like the one reproduced in fig. previous.
54. Fragments of decoration of the upper area of the room (35).
56. Room (35): fragment of epistyle rendered in perspective, with a vase serving as an acrotery.
57. Room (36): another floor of cocciopesto dating back to the Republican age and adorned only with scattered black and white tiles.
58. Room (36), N wall with the square window open onto (35): the decoration belongs to the same phase as that of the adjoining room, reproduced in figs. previous ones (III 'candelabra' style).

59. Room (36): the wall E with the large hole left by the passage of seekers who have penetrated the room. Red plinth, high black plinth with panels divided by metal candelabra; yellow middle area containing two panels with garlands; black frieze and remains of the upper area.
60. Room (36), wall E, section N: detail of the yellow panel with hanging garland and festoon. III "candelabra" style.
61. Room (36), SE corner: detail of the garlands hanging in the yellow panels. You can see the imprinted lines to facilitate the execution of the garland.
63. Room (36), wall W with remains of a fresco (III "candelabra" style): red plinth, black plinth, yellow middle area.

62. Room (36), S wall: red plinth, high black plinth; middle area with central aedicule on a white background with black predella and yellow side panels with hanging garland; black frieze; remains of the upper area on a white background.

64. Environment (36). The collapsed fragments of the black frieze allow us to better read the decoration: a chain of circles engraved with a compass containing plant elements. Typical of this phase (III "candelabra" style), datable to the beginning of the imperial age, are also the two borders on a white background on which horizontal lines of different colors simulate frames.
65. Room (36): collapsed fragments of a yellow side panel with the knotted garland hanging.

66. A series of sporadic fragments of fresco, mosaic, stucco, temporarily deposited in the room (45) of the house, are in this photo and in fig. here is a white carpet with a network of diamonds probably assignable to the second style.
67. Fragment of floor with white beaten and border with bands of black and white tesserae, also assignable to the II style.
68. Fragment of a fresco with a mystical cyst containing the phallus hidden by a cloth and pomegranate.
69. Fragment of a fresco with a beamed ceiling seen in perspective.
70. Fragments of fresco pertaining to a frieze with a warrior running to the left, rendered with rapid and sure strokes of color that plastically construct the figure.
71. Fragment of a fresco with a faux marble panel.
72. Fragments of a fresco with a male figure flying on a yellow background.
73. Fragments of a stucco frieze with an aedicule and a rectangular panel containing a palmette.
74. Eaves box with lion's head covered with stucco; the lateral raised palmettes are also stucco, covering the palmettes made by moulding from a tired matrix. 79 N60835
75. Lion-headed gutter box, covered with a high layer of white stucco and adorned with palmettes. 79 N60836
1. Vestibule (1), floor: carpet of white tesserae with larger tesserae, of coloured limestone. The threshold towards the atrium is meandering and square. III style.
2. Atrium (2), view from the W with the wide opening of the vestibule and brick and opus mixtum walls (reticulated with brick mirrors).
3. Atrium (2), S wall, section E: the latticed masonry with brick mirrors has not received any cladding.

4. Atrium (2), detail of the black and white mosaic floor: carpet of black tesserae arranged in an oblique warp with small scattered white tesserae; border of white tesserae arranged in a straight warp, marginal flounce of black tesserae arranged in an oblique warp, meandering and square threshold.
6. On the mosaic amphora reproduced here, the inscription is G(ari) f(los) scom(bri)/Scauri (Pompeii, Antiquarium, inv. 15189). AFS 60945

5. Detail of the mosaic torn from the corners of the impluvium (Pompeii, Antiquarium, inv. 15188) which reproduces an amphora on which the inscription Liqua(men)/flos is shown in mosaic: this is the same inscription that sometimes appears on amphorae very similar to the one made here, single-handled, with a wide foot and a high neck, on which the name of the manufacturer is also frequently reported,  A. Umbricius Scaurus, (for this inscription and the following cf. Anneé Epigrafique, 1992, no. 278).
7. Amphora with inscription G(arì) f(los) sco[m(bri)] / Scauri, / ex offi[ci]/na Scau/ri (Pompeii, Antiquarium, inv. 15196).
8. Fragmentary mosaic amphora (Pompeii, Antiquarium, inv. 15191) with inscription remains. AFS 60948

9. Wing (9), wall E with masonry in opus uncertain with brick recurrences, covered with a fresco of the second style with a black background. The large hole is the trace of the passage of prospectors.
10. Wing (9), S wall with remains of a fresco of the second style (orthostats with a black background). 79 N51018
1. The boundary wall of the house along the Vicolo dei Soprastanti; the masonry in opus incerta is punctuated by limestone semi-columns with Doric capitals of tuff.
2. Vestibule (1): fragments of relief decoration of stucco of the first style, deposited in the room.

3. Porticoed courtyard (2), portico E, section N: detail of the cocciopesto floor dating back to the Republican age. Slivers of black limestone and small white tesserae are arranged in regular rows; At the column, the carpet is marked by a threshold formed by small white tesserae spaced out from each other and bedded at the vertices, which enclose a barely distinguishable cross motif.

4. Porticoed courtyard (2), N portico, N wall: in correspondence with room (7) the III style decoration on the other walls (see figs. below) has been replaced by a fresco of the IV style, of which a twisted candelabrum can be recognized in the black middle area, while in the red upper area there is a tripod.

5. Porticoed courtyard (2), portico E, wall E, section N: on the high black plinth adorned with plants, of not particularly accurate execution, the middle area contains in the center an aedicule with a landscape painting, closed at the bottom by a black predella on which birds are painted; The side panels are red. The decoration can be assigned to the final phase of the III style.

6. Courtyard portico (2), portico E, wall E, section S: in the black plinth panels with plants alternate with narrow compartments; In the center of the middle area is a large aedicule containing a sacred landscape, closed at the bottom by a black predella, the side panels are red. The slender ornamentation of the columns and the crowning of the aedicule allows the decoration to be assigned to the last phase of the III style.

7. Porticoed courtyard (2): fragments of pluteus decorated with yellow and red bipartite scales are deposited in the room, assignable to the II style. Corded strips imprinted in the still fresh plaster were used by the decorator to outline the motif. The fragment on the left can instead be assigned to the IV style.
8. Room (7), floor: the transition area between the porticoed courtyard (2) and the room (8) is emphasized by the wall and floor decoration (see also the following figs).

9. Room (7), floor, detail of the central section with the mat that emphasizes the entrance to the room (8): within a rectangle bordered by bands with networks of diamonds outlined in white tiles, with black tiles at the crossing points, polychrome marble slabs are framed by scattered white tiles. The rectangle then bears pairs of pecking birds on the four sides. Room (26), wall E with decoration of the fourth style in a two-part scheme: above the plinth, red, the plinth of the same colour has a compartment with a plan in the centre, while in the side panels there are stylised aedicules between bands with carpet edges. Room (28): on the S wall there is the lararium, often divided between a lower area, with snakes on either side of an altar, and an upper area, in which the Lares are represented (the one on the left is almost completely lost), who assist at the sacrifice at an altar. Room (32), wall O: fragments relocated in situ of a rare and rich wall decoration of the IV style, at the base of which ran an opus sectile plinth (see fig. 92), resting on a floor in the same technique of which the remains can be recognized along the E and S walls of the room. Oecus (44), floor: a section of the mosaic floor was laid on the ground after detachment, with a carpet of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp, a border with black and white bands and a flounce of white tesserae arranged in a straight warp, older than the wall decoration and still attributable to the Republican age.

Oecus (44), N wall: the IV style decoration of the room, which is located on the first underground floor, has a black monochrome background and, as in other rooms on this floor, is not of great quality. However, unlike the rooms of the fourth style examined so far, which, although presenting monochrome decorations of pleasant effect, are not distinguished by their level, for this oecus, as for the apsidal hall (62) (see below), a more accurate decoration has been chosen, as evidenced by the abundance of almost miniature motifs that embellish the walls. It is also important to underline that the greater decorative commitment reserved for these rooms does not mean that higher-level workshops are active here: on the contrary, these are achievements that are fully part of the panorama of contemporary decoration, in which they stand out for the care of execution, but from which they do not detach themselves for a real qualitative difference.
